did_you_know.text: The heading identifies the psalm as “A psalm of David” and dedicates it to the “chief musician.” The heading alone does not allow us to determine with certainty what stage of David’s life the psalm comes from.
The psalm opens with a personal and direct request: the poet asks the Lord to hear his voice and preserve his life from the fear of the enemy.
This verse contrasts the “secret counsel of evildoers” with the request for the Lord’s protection: in the face of the wicked gathering in secret, the poet asks God to hide and protect him.
The wicked are portrayed through images of war involving speech and weapons: they “sharpen their tongues like a sword” and aim their words like arrows.
The plot is portrayed as hidden and sudden: the wicked shoot from concealed places, attack the innocent, and have no fear of being discovered.
These verses describe how the wicked encourage one another in planning evil and try to conceal their traps, thinking that no one will see what they are doing.
The turning point in the psalm comes when the Lord turns the image of the arrow against the wicked: the sudden arrow becomes a symbol of the plot turning against its creators.
The wicked’s words, which earlier served as weapons of attack, become a source of trouble for them; thus, the psalm presents the principle of retribution—the punishment fits the crime.
After the wicked are defeated, people recognize God’s work and understand its significance; the community therefore responds with awe and acknowledgment.
The conclusion presents the central contrast with the plots of the wicked: the righteous rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him, while those who are upright in heart glory in him.
